summary: A Buddhist studies scholar, Genro succeeded Hakuin Ekaku and served as the first seat (第一座) at Myoshin-ji.
Genryu Kagoshima, a Buddhist studies scholar, studied at Komazawa University from around 1931 to 1934. He later served as a professor there from circa 1958 to 1983 and taught William M. Bodiford.

Gensho Imanari specialized in Japanology and Buddhist studies, earning his degrees and PhD at Waseda University. He was an assistant professor at Kokushikan University (c. 1959-1965) and professor emeritus at Rissho University (1980-1996).
A scholar of Buddhist studies, Genshu Watanabe studied at Toyo University and trained under Daiun Sogaku Harada as his dharma heir.
Genzao worked in Buddhist studies and Tibetology. He studied at Dzogchen Monastery until 1950, having studied under traditional teachers Jiangze Rinpoche in 1948 and Kalu Rinpoche.

Geo Widengren worked in Iranian, Central Asian, and religious studies. He studied at Stockholm and Uppsala universities (doctorate under Henrik Samuel Nyberg), was Professor of History of Religions at Uppsala (1940-1973), and served as president of the IAHR.

Geoff Childs is a scholar of Tibetology and history/archaeology who studied at Indiana University Bloomington (PhD) under Tsetan Chonjore. He held positions at the Australian National University and Washington University in St. Louis.

Geoffrey Barstow is a scholar of Tibetology, Buddhist studies, and religious studies. He studied at Hampshire College, Kathmandu University, and the University of Virginia (PhD), and was appointed assistant professor of religious studies at Oregon State University circa 2013.

Geoffrey Goble, a scholar of Buddhist studies, sinology, and religious studies, earned an MA from the University of Virginia and a PhD from Indiana University Bloomington. He served as Assistant Professor of Religious Studies at the University of Oklahoma.

Geoffrey Samuel specialized in Tibetology, religious studies, and Buddhist studies, earning his PhD at Cambridge under Tambiah, Wilson, and Leach. He held professorships at Newcastle, Lancaster, and Cardiff, alongside affiliations with Berkeley, Manchester, SOAS, and Sydney.

Georg Buddruss was a scholar of Indology, linguistics, and Iranian and Central Asian studies. He earned his doctorate under Paul Thieme at Goethe University Frankfurt, studied at the University of Tübingen, and served as professor at Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz (1963-1995).

Georg Bühler was an Indologist and linguist who completed his PhD at Göttingen. He served as a professor in Mumbai and at Elphinstone College, worked in the Bombay Presidency Educational Department, and held a chair at the University of Vienna from 1880.

Georg Christoph Lichtenberg studied at the University of Göttingen from circa 1763 to 1769 and worked there from around 1769 to 1799 in philosophy and other fields, teaching Wilhelm and Alexander von Humboldt and Carl Friedrich Gauss.

Georg Curtius was a linguist and Indologist who studied at Bonn and Berlin. He taught at Dresden, held professorships at Charles University (1849-1854) and Kiel University (1854-1862), and was professor of classical philology at the University of Leipzig (1862-1885).
Georg Forster was an Indologist who studied at Petrischule. He held academic posts at Vilnius University (1784-1787) and Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz (circa 1788-1793).

Georg Freytag was a linguist who studied at the University of Göttingen and under Antoine-Isaac Silvestre de Sacy. He held positions at Göttingen and Königsberg before serving as professor of Oriental languages at the University of Bonn from 1819 to 1861.
Georg Friedrich Grotefend was a scholar of Iranian, Central Asian studies, and linguistics who studied at the Lessing-Gymnasium and the University of Göttingen (circa 1795-1797).

Georg Heinrich Pertz was a historian who studied under Arnold Hermann Ludwig Heeren at the University of Göttingen from around 1813 to 1818. He served as head of the Prussian State Library from circa 1842 to 1873.

Georg Huth was a scholar of Tibetology, Indology, and Iranian and Central Asian studies. He studied at the University of Leipzig (c. 1885-1889) and later held a post at Humboldt University of Berlin (c. 1891-1906).

Georg Kaibel, a scholar in linguistics, history, and archaeology, held posts at the University of Rostock (c. 1879-1882), University of Breslau (c. 1882-1883), University of Greifswald (c. 1883-1886), and University of Göttingen (c. 1897-1901).
